notes.meaning: God speaks to Moses while Israel is camped on the plains of Moab across from Jericho. This is the final stretch of their journey before entering Canaan, where the Lord gives final instructions about how they will live in the land.

The Lord orders the other tribes to give some of their own towns and grazing lands to the tribe of Levi. Because the Levites served as priests and religious workers, they did not receive a large region of their own, but were given places to live throughout the whole nation.

The Levites were to live in these towns with their families, while the open land around the walls was set aside for their cattle, sheep, and other animals. This allowed them to feed their livestock without owning large farms.
God defines the boundaries of the pastureland outside each town wall. The ground extended outward from the city center, providing plenty of space on every side for the Levites' herds and gardens.

Out of the towns given to the Levites, six were chosen as cities of refuge where someone who accidentally killed another person could run for safety. The Levites were also given forty-two other towns, making a total of forty-eight.
All forty-eight cities, along with their pastures, were taken from the other tribes in a fair way. Larger tribes with bigger territories gave more towns, while smaller tribes gave fewer.

God tells Moses that once Israel crosses the Jordan River, they must set up safe towns for anyone who causes an accidental death. These cities of refuge were meant for a person who killed someone without planning to do so and without any hatred.

These towns protected the runner from the dead person's closest relative, who was expected to avenge the family's loss. The shelter kept the runner alive until a public court could hear the facts and decide if it was really an accident.

Three refuge cities were placed east of the Jordan River and three were placed on the west side in the land of Canaan. Spreading them out across the country made sure that a safe place was never too far away for anyone in danger.

The right to flee to these cities applied equally to native Israelites and to foreigners living among them. God's law provided the same fair protection and justice to everyone, no matter where they were born.

If someone strikes another person with an iron tool, a heavy stone, or a wooden weapon and that person dies, the act is counted as murder. Using an object that is clearly deadly proves that the attacker intended to kill, so the city of refuge could not protect them.

The victim's nearest relative was authorized to carry out the death sentence against a convicted murderer. Once the person was legally proven guilty, justice was completed by taking the murderer's life.

Killing someone out of hatred, waiting in hiding to attack, or striking a deadly blow in anger is classified as murder. In every case where real malice is shown, the killer must be put to death rather than granted shelter.

A sudden push without anger, an object thrown without looking, or a heavy stone dropped without bad intentions are true accidents. If the two people were not enemies and there was no plan to do harm, the law treated the death as manslaughter rather than murder.

The community judges the case between the runner and the dead person's relative. If the judges find that the death was accidental, they return the person safely to the city of refuge, where he must live until the current high priest dies.

If the accidental killer ever wanders outside the safety zone of the city, the avenger can kill him without being charged with a crime. The runner had to accept this period of exile until the high priest's death, which paid the debt of the incident and allowed him to go home in peace.
These legal rules were not temporary tips, but permanent laws for all generations across Israel. They established a lasting standard for separating intentional murder from tragic accidents.

A person accused of murder could only be put to death if at least two witnesses testified against him. The word of a single witness was never enough to take someone's life, which protected the innocent from false accusations or personal grudges.

Israel was strictly forbidden from taking money to spare the life of a convicted murderer. A murderer's life could not be bought off with cash, because human life is sacred and only execution satisfied the law.

No payment could be accepted to let an accidental killer leave the city of refuge early either. The person had to complete their time of exile until the high priest died, showing that even accidental bloodshed carried a serious cost.

Unpunished murder stains and ruins the land itself in the eyes of God. Atonement, which means making things right after a wrong, could only be made for shed blood by the execution of the guilty murderer.

The people were warned not to ruin their homeland by tolerating injustice and murder, because the Lord Himself lived among them in the tabernacle. God's holy presence required the community to keep their society pure and just.
